title: Retries with backoff, timeouts, pagination, uploads with progress
summary: A production client retries only what is safe to repeat, with exponential backoff, jitter and the server's Retry-After; pages with server-issued cursors instead of offsets; and reports progress by counting streamed bytes, or by uploading in parts, because fetch has no upload progress events.

examples.title: Retries: what to retry, how long to wait, and the Idempotency-Key

annotations.note: sleep and random are injected, so the example runs instantly and prints the same delays every time. In production they are a setTimeout promise and Math.random; in tests, no fake timers needed.

Retry what may go away: timeouts (408), rate limits (429) and server-side trouble (500, 502, 503, 504). A 400, 401, 404 or 422 will say the same thing next time. The idempotent methods are the ones HTTP defines as safe to repeat; POST and PATCH are not.

A POST is repeatable only with an Idempotency-Key: the server stores the result under the key and answers a repeat with the stored result instead of charging twice. The header is an IETF draft and a widespread convention; the server has to implement it.

A deadline per attempt, so one hung connection doesn't use up the whole budget. In real code, merge it with the caller's signal through AbortSignal.any() so a cancel stops the retries too. clone(), because sending a request consumes its body: the same Request can't be sent twice.
Only "no response" is retried here: a network TypeError or this attempt's TimeoutError. A caller's abort or a bug in your own code is not a reason to try again.
A POST without a key that got no response has an unknown outcome: the server may have committed it. Saying so is the honest answer; retrying blindly is how users get charged twice.

Exponential backoff with full jitter: a random wait below a ceiling that doubles per attempt, so clients that failed together don't retry together. A Retry-After header wins. It can also be an HTTP date, which needs Date.parse and an injected clock; this sketch handles the seconds form only.
The key is created once per user intent (one click on Pay) and reused by every retry of that intent. A new key per attempt would defeat it.

examples.title: Offset vs cursor pagination, and following the server's next link

annotations.note: Offset paging counts rows: "skip 2". When a row is inserted in front, everything shifts by one, so page 2 repeats order 4. A deleted row shifts the other way and one is skipped. PostgreSQL also has to read and throw away every skipped row.

Cursor (keyset) paging remembers a position: "older than order 4". Inserts and deletes elsewhere don't move it, and an index on id finds the start directly (sql.indexes.stats-pagination). The cursor is opaque: the client treats it as a token, so the server may change its contents later.
The client follows the next URL the server returns until it is null, and never builds page URLs itself. An async generator fetches a page only when the loop asks for it, and break stops it.
The same insert in both runs. Offset shows 4 twice; cursor shows every order exactly once (the new one appears at the top on the next refresh).

examples.title: Download progress from the body stream; upload progress in parts

annotations.note: Progress is measured in bytes. Each of these Turkish letters is 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 30000 characters are 60000 bytes: compute progress from file.size, not from string length.

Reading the body yourself instead of calling json() or blob(): each read() returns the next chunk the network delivered, so the count of bytes so far is the progress. Chunk sizes are up to the browser; here the fake server fixes them at 16 KiB.

Content-Length can be missing (a chunked response) or count the compressed bytes when Content-Encoding is gzip, while the stream yields decompressed ones. Treat it as a hint and fall back to an indeterminate progress bar.

fetch exposes no upload progress at all. Sending a file in parts gives progress that means "the server has this much", and a failed part is retried alone. S3 multipart uploads and the tus protocol work this way.
Blob.slice cuts at byte offsets and can split a multi-byte character. That is fine for upload parts, which the server reassembles before anyone decodes them; never decode a part on its own.

use_cases: Mobile and flaky networks: retry idempotent requests with backoff, give non-idempotent ones a key
Rate-limited third-party APIs: honour 429 and Retry-After instead of hammering
Infinite scroll and exports over live data: cursor pagination with server-issued next links
Large file uploads (videos, CSV imports) with a progress bar and resume after a dropped connection
strengths: Composable platform pieces: AbortSignal for deadlines, Request.clone() for re-sending, async generators for pages, streams for progress
Injected sleep and randomness make retry logic testable in microseconds, without fake timers
Server-issued cursors let the server change its paging scheme without a client release
Uploading in parts survives flaky connections: only the failed part is sent again
weaknesses: fetch has no built-in retry, no upload progress and no pagination helper; each is code you own and test
Retries multiply across layers and can turn a short outage into an overload the clients caused themselves
Cursor pagination can't jump to page 7 or show a total cheaply
Download progress depends on Content-Length, which compression and chunked responses make unreliable

pitfalls.title: Retrying requests that aren't safe to repeat
pitfalls.detail: A POST that timed out may have succeeded. Retry it only with an Idempotency-Key the server honours, created once per user action.
pitfalls.bad: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { try { return await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body }); } catch {} }
pitfalls.good:
const headers = { "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID() }; // once per click
await send(doFetch, new Request(url, { method: "POST", body, headers }), policy);

pitfalls.title: Retrying 4xx responses
pitfalls.detail: 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 won't change on a retry. Only 408 and 429 among the 4xx codes mean "try again later".

pitfalls.title: Fixed delays, or no cap
pitfalls.detail: Every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment. Use exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum number of attempts, and the caller's deadline.

pitfalls.title: Retrying at every layer
pitfalls.detail: Three attempts each in the browser, in a backend-for-frontend and in the service behind it make up to 27 requests to the last service. TanStack Query already retries failed queries three times by default; don't add a retrying fetch wrapper under it.

pitfalls.title: Offset pagination over data that changes
pitfalls.detail: Inserts duplicate items across pages and deletes skip them. Use a keyset cursor for feeds, exports and infinite scroll.

quiz.q: POST /payments timed out with no response. What does the client know?
options: Nothing: the server may or may not have committed it
quiz.why: A lost response says nothing about the server side. Without an Idempotency-Key the only safe move is to report the unknown outcome, or check the order's status.

quiz.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: So clients that failed at the same moment don't all retry at the same moment
quiz.why: Without jitter, synchronized clients form waves that hit the recovering server together. A random wait spreads them out.

quiz.q: A list pages with ?offset=. A new item is inserted at the top between page 1 and page 2. What does the user see?
options: The last item of page 1 again at the top of page 2
quiz.why: Everything shifts down by one, so offset 2 now starts at the item that was at offset 1. A delete does the opposite and skips one.

quiz.q: How can a browser app show upload progress for a 500 MB file?
options: XMLHttpRequest's upload progress events, or uploading in parts with fetch
Reading response.body while the upload runs
quiz.why: fetch has no upload progress events. xhr.upload fires progress events; parts give progress that the server has confirmed.

body:
## Concept

The plain client from the first lesson becomes production-grade by adding four
behaviours, each a small piece of code you own.

**Retries.** Retry a request only when the failure may go away *and* repeating it is
safe. "May go away": no response at all, a timed-out attempt, 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 and
504. "Safe": the method is idempotent (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE), or the request
carries an `Idempotency-Key` that the server uses to recognise a repeat. Wait between
attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `Retry-After` (seconds or an HTTP
date), and stop at a maximum number of attempts or at the caller's deadline.

**Timeouts.** Two of them: one per attempt (`AbortSignal.timeout`), and one for the whole
operation, which is usually the caller's signal. Combine them with `AbortSignal.any()`.

**Pagination.** Offset paging (`?offset=40`) is simple and lets users jump to a page, but
it shifts when rows are inserted or deleted, and it gets slower with depth. Cursor paging
(`?cursor=…`, keyset in SQL) is stable and fast, and the server should hand out the next
URL or cursor so the client never constructs one. Some APIs put that URL in a `Link`
header with `rel="next"`; reading it cross-origin requires the server to list `Link` in
`Access-Control-Expose-Headers`.

**Progress.** Download progress comes from reading `response.body` chunk by chunk and
counting bytes. Uploads are the gap: fetch has no upload progress events.
`XMLHttpRequest` still has them, and uploading in parts gives progress that the server
has confirmed:

```ts
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.upload.addEventListener("progress", (e) => {
  if (e.lengthComputable) bar.value = e.loaded / e.total;
});
xhr.open("POST", "/api/uploads");
xhr.send(file);
```

A listener on `xhr.upload` makes a cross-origin request preflighted (next lesson). A
`ReadableStream` request body (with `duplex: "half"`) lets you count bytes as fetch reads
them, but that measures what the browser took, not what the server received, and support
differs between browsers.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: urllib3's `Retry(total=..., backoff_factor=..., status_forcelist=...)`
  retries only `allowed_methods`, which by default excludes POST and PATCH, and respects
  `Retry-After`: the same policy as `send()` here.
- **C**: the curl tool's `--retry` treats a timeout and HTTP 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504
  (plus Cloudflare's 522 and 524) as transient, doubles its wait between attempts, and
  lets `Retry-After` override the wait.
- **Go**: the same loop, with `context` instead of `AbortSignal` (go.services.retries). A
  Go request body is also read once; `http.Request.GetBody` returns a fresh copy, the job
  `Request.clone()` does here. `http.Transport` itself replays a request after a network
  error on a reused connection only if it counts as idempotent: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE,
  or any request with an `Idempotency-Key` header.
- **Java**: teams reach for Resilience4j or Spring Retry. In the browser there is no
  standard library for this: write the loop, or let TanStack Query retry queries.
- **JS**: TanStack Query retries failed queries three times with exponential backoff by
  default and doesn't retry mutations; keep fetch-level retries out of code that runs under
  it.

## Design notes

Put the policy in one place, the API client, as data: attempts, base delay, which
statuses, which methods. Callers shouldn't sprinkle retry loops. Inject the clock, the
sleep and the random source; deterministic tests of retry logic are otherwise slow and
flaky.

Retry at one layer only, and give the whole operation a budget: a deadline signal from the
caller, merged with the per-attempt timeout. When the user navigates away, the cancel
should stop the waiting as well as the request.

Idempotency is a contract with the server. The client creates the key per user intent and
keeps it for that intent's retries (store it with the pending form if a reload must not
duplicate the order); the server stores the outcome under the key, typically with a unique
constraint and an upsert (sql.modifying.returning-upsert), and replays it.

For pagination, let the server own the cursor format and return the next link; for
progress, report what you can measure honestly: bytes read, parts acknowledged, or an
indeterminate spinner.
